name: Diagnostic Feedback and Performance Management in Salta
nameLocal: Retroalimentación diagnóstica y gestión del desempeño en Salta
summaryShort: Salta experiment combining student diagnostic feedback for schools with management tools and training for principals and supervisors.
summaryLong: The Salta diagnostic feedback and performance-management intervention tested whether assessment information alone, or information plus management capacity, could improve public primary school outcomes. Schools received reports on students' math and reading performance; a second treatment group also received online tools and training to help principals and supervisors create and monitor school improvement plans.
objectives: Help principals use student assessment information
Strengthen school-management capacity
Reduce grade repetition and overage
Improve instruction and school climate
mechanisms: The diagnostic-feedback group received math and reading assessment reports. The performance-management group received those reports plus tools and training for principals and supervisors to develop and monitor progress against school improvement plans.
coverage: Experiment in 396 public primary schools in Salta, Argentina
impactSummary: The randomized evaluation found that diagnostic feedback alone had null or adverse effects on student performance in school, while feedback combined with performance-management tools and training reduced grade repetition, especially among cohorts with greater exposure.

keyOutcomes.effect: Performance-management treatment reduced repetition by 1.5 percentage points relative to control and 3.5 percentage points relative to diagnostic feedback alone
Higher repetition and overage rates than control after two years
No statistically significant achievement effects, though small-to-moderate effects could not be ruled out

evaluations.authors: de Hoyos, Rafael; Djaker, Sharnic; Ganimian, Alejandro J.; Holland, Peter A.
evaluations.title: The impact of combining performance-management tools and training with diagnostic feedback in public schools: Experimental evidence from Argentina
evaluations.keyFinding: Diagnostic feedback alone did not improve outcomes, but combining feedback with performance-management tools and training reduced grade repetition.

name: PODER Dropout Prevention Pilot
nameLocal: Programa de Oportunidades y Desarrollo para Evitar Riesgos
summaryShort: Mexico City upper-secondary dropout-prevention pilot combining cognitive behavioral therapy workshops with math tutoring for at-risk students.
summaryLong: PODER was designed by Mexico's Secretariat of Public Education with the World Bank to reduce upper-secondary dropout. The pilot targeted first-year upper-secondary students at risk of dropping out and combined cognitive behavioral therapy-based socioemotional workshops with math tutoring. The program is important for the database because the rigorous evaluation documents both implementation limits and heterogeneous effects.
objectives: Reduce upper-secondary dropout
Improve socioemotional skills
Strengthen math readiness for at-risk students
Test a scalable school-based dropout-prevention model
mechanisms: The intervention offered voluntary CBT-based workshops focused on decision-making, emotion management, and future orientation, complemented by math tutoring for students with accumulated academic gaps.
coverage: More than 5,000 youth in 20 public upper-secondary schools in Mexico City
impactSummary: The randomized field experiment found some evidence of improved socioemotional skills, but no intention-to-treat effects on math outcomes or future attendance. Low take-up and implementation constraints appear to have limited impacts; exploratory analyses suggest heterogeneous effects by participation.

evaluations.journal: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper

name: Classroom Observation and Coaching in Ceara
nameLocal: Observação de sala de aula e coaching no Ceará
summaryShort: Ceara secondary-school program using classroom observation feedback and expert coaching to improve teacher practice and student learning.
summaryLong: The Ceara classroom observation and coaching program tested whether teachers could improve practice through benchmarked classroom-observation feedback and access to expert coaching. The state implemented the intervention over one school year in secondary schools, using pedagogical coordinators and remote coaching support. The evaluation is a major Latin American example of teacher professional development with direct measures of classroom practice and student learning.
objectives: Improve teacher effectiveness
Increase instructional time and student engagement
Use observation feedback to guide teacher professional development
Raise student learning in secondary schools

name: Juancito Pinto School Grant
summaryShort: An annual cash transfer of 200 bolivianos paid to students in Bolivian public schools, conditional on enrollment and regular attendance, created in 2006 to promote school entry, retention and completion.
summaryLong: The Bono Juancito Pinto was introduced by the government of Evo Morales in October 2006 as a yearly cash payment to children enrolled in public schools, with the explicit objective of improving enrollment, retention and completion rates. It initially covered the first years of primary school and was progressively expanded so that by 2014 it reached all grades of public primary and secondary education. The benefit is a flat 200 bolivianos per student per year, roughly 29 US dollars, delivered at school pay points with support from the armed forces and financed largely with transfers from state owned enterprises, especially the oil and gas company YPFB. It is one of the largest social programs in Bolivia by number of beneficiaries and has been paid every year since 2006.
objectives: Increase enrollment in public primary and secondary schools
Reduce dropout and promote school year completion
Lower the direct costs of schooling for poor households
Discourage child labor by compensating part of the opportunity cost of schooling
mechanisms: Each year the government issues a supreme decree authorizing the payment, financed mainly by contributions from public enterprises. Students enrolled in public schools who have attended regularly during the school year receive a single payment of 200 bolivianos, usually handed over at the school in the presence of a parent or guardian, with the armed forces supporting logistics and payment in remote areas. School directors certify enrollment and attendance, which constitutes the conditionality.
coverage: In 2023 the program paid 2,297,296 students, about 99.7 percent of the target population of 2.34 million, with a budget of 477 million bolivianos funded by 28 public enterprises.
impactSummary: A peer reviewed quasi-experimental study found that the transfer raises the probability of school enrollment by about one percentage point on average but has no sizeable effect on child labor, which the authors attribute to the small size of the transfer relative to the opportunity cost of older children's time. Other analyses associate the program with small reductions in extreme poverty and inequality. There is no experimental evaluation.

No sizeable effect on the incidence of child labor

name: Avelino Siñani-Elizardo Pérez Education Law
nameLocal: Ley de la Educación No 070 Avelino Siñani-Elizardo Pérez
summaryShort: Bolivia's framework education law of December 2010, which reorganized the entire education system around decolonizing, intracultural, intercultural, plurilingual, community based and productive education aligned with the plurinational state.
summaryLong: Law No 070, enacted on 20 December 2010, replaced the 1994 education reform law and refounded the Bolivian education system as the Sistema Educativo Plurinacional. The law declares education a fundamental right that the state must guarantee at all levels in a universal, free, integral and intercultural way without discrimination, and it is named after Avelino Siñani and Elizardo Pérez, founders of the indigenous school of Warisata in the 1930s. It organizes the system into regular education, alternative and special education, and higher education for professional training, and mandates that schooling be intracultural, intercultural and plurilingual, recognizing indigenous languages alongside Spanish.
objectives: Establish education as a universal, free and compulsory right guaranteed by the state
Decolonize education and root curricula in Bolivia's indigenous cultures, languages and knowledge
Link schooling to productive and community life through a sociocommunity productive education model
Consolidate the plurinational state by promoting intracultural, intercultural and plurilingual education at all levels
mechanisms: The law restructures governance of the whole education system under state and social oversight, creates the plurinational education system with its three subsystems, and mandates new curricular bases that combine universal knowledge with indigenous knowledge systems. Implementation proceeded through a new national base curriculum and regionalized curricula rolled out in stages starting in 2013, complementary in-service teacher training, and the introduction of a technical humanistic upper secondary degree. Indigenous education councils participate in curriculum development for their peoples.
coverage: The law governs the entire Bolivian education system, covering all students in regular, alternative and special, and higher education, which means several million students and the whole teaching force.
impactSummary: There is no rigorous impact evaluation of the law or of its sociocommunity productive education model. Available literature is legal, descriptive and qualitative, discussing implementation, the decolonization agenda and tensions between national curricula and local indigenous curricula. Its causal effects on learning, attainment or equity have not been measured.

name: National Literacy Program Yes I Can
nameLocal: Programa Nacional de Alfabetización Yo Sí Puedo
summaryShort: A mass adult literacy campaign launched by the Morales government in 2006 using the Cuban Yo Sí Puedo audiovisual method, after which Bolivia declared itself free of illiteracy in December 2008.
summaryLong: The Programa Nacional de Alfabetización was launched in 2006 with technical assistance from Cuba and financial support from Venezuela, using the Cuban Yo Sí Puedo method of audiovisual literacy lessons delivered over about 65 sessions. A census carried out in 2006 and 2007 identified 823,256 illiterate adults, and by the end of the campaign the government reported that 819,417 people had completed the program, including graduates in Aymara and Quechua. On 20 December 2008 Bolivia declared itself a territory free of illiteracy, citing an illiteracy rate below the 4 percent threshold used by UNESCO. The campaign was followed by a post-literacy program, Yo Sí Puedo Seguir, managed by the Ministry of Education.
objectives: Eradicate adult illiteracy in Bolivia within roughly 30 months
Reach rural, indigenous and female populations with the highest illiteracy rates
Provide literacy instruction in Spanish and in Aymara and Quechua
Create the basis for continuing adult education through post-literacy programs
mechanisms: The program used the Cuban Yo Sí Puedo methodology, in which facilitators guide small groups of adult learners through a sequence of about 65 audiovisual classes shown on television sets and video players installed in community learning points. Cuba provided advisers, teaching materials and equipment, Venezuela provided financing, and Bolivian facilitators ran the local sessions. Literacy points were set up throughout the country, including versions of the materials in Aymara and Quechua.
coverage: 819,417 adults completed the program between 2006 and 2008, out of 823,256 illiterate adults identified in the baseline census, including 24,699 graduates in Aymara and 13,599 in Quechua.
impactSummary: Official figures show near universal completion among the identified illiterate population, and Bolivia declared itself free of illiteracy in 2008. An independent quasi-experimental assessment by researchers at Fundación ARU questioned how much of the decline in illiteracy can be attributed to the program and whether illiteracy actually fell below the 4 percent threshold, finding more modest effects on basic reading and writing skills than official graduation counts suggest. No experimental evaluation exists.

name: High Performance Schools
summaryShort: A national network of selective public boarding schools for high achieving students in the last three grades of secondary school, created by Peru's Ministry of Education in 2014 and operating in all 25 regions.
summaryLong: The Colegios de Alto Rendimiento are selective public boarding schools that serve high achieving students in grades 3 to 5 of secondary education. Building on the Colegio Mayor Secundario Presidente del Perú created in Lima in 2009, the Ministry of Education established the COAR network in 2014 and expanded it so that every one of Peru's 25 regions has a COAR. Students are admitted through a competitive two stage process that prioritizes top performers from public schools, and they receive full board, an extended school day, intensive English, and a curriculum aligned with the International Baccalaureate diploma. The model is one of the most resource intensive per student interventions in Peruvian basic education and has been the subject of a joint research agenda between the ministry and the development bank CAF.
objectives: Offer a high quality public secondary education option to high achieving students, especially from public schools and poorer regions
Develop academic, artistic and socioemotional talent through a boarding school model with an International Baccalaureate aligned curriculum
Improve access of talented public school students to higher education and high return careers
Decentralize educational excellence by operating one COAR in each of the 25 regions
mechanisms: Students who finished second grade of secondary school with top grades or who placed in academic competitions apply through an annual admission process that combines a standardized test phase with an assessment of skills and interviews. Admitted students move to residential campuses where they study an extended day under the IB framework, with housing, food, materials and tutoring fully funded by the state. Each region operates one COAR under ministry guidelines.
coverage: 25 schools, one per region, serving about 6,700 students in grades 3 to 5 of secondary education as of the early 2020s.
impactSummary: A regression discontinuity evaluation by the Ministry of Education and CAF comparing marginally admitted and marginally rejected applicants of the 2016 cohort found no detectable differences in mathematics and reading test performance or in measured socioemotional skills three years after entry, but a 14.5 percentage point higher intention to attend university. Follow up analysis of education and labor market outcomes found higher immediate university enrollment, a 7 percentage point higher probability of choosing high return careers, and formal wage gains averaging about 4 percent, reaching 16 percent for the earliest cohort observed longest in the labor market. A separate GRADE study evaluated design and implementation qualitatively, reporting strong engagement alongside infrastructure problems and staff overload.

name: I Learn at Home
summaryShort: Peru's national multichannel remote learning strategy during the COVID-19 school closures, launched in April 2020 and delivered through television, radio, a web platform and WhatsApp, later wound down as schools returned to in person classes through 2022.
summaryLong: Aprendo en Casa was created by the Ministry of Education in roughly two weeks after the March 2020 closure of schools and was launched on 6 April 2020 as a free national distance education service. It combined daily programming on open signal television and on hundreds of radio stations, including programming in indigenous languages, with a web platform organized by grade and competencies, using WhatsApp and phone contact between teachers and families for follow up. The ministry reported in 2020 that around 90 percent of students had connected with the strategy in some form. As in person and blended schooling resumed in 2021 and 2022, the strategy was redefined through the guidelines for Aprendo en Casa, Aprendo en Escuela and Aprendo en Comunidad and was phased out as a stand alone national remote schooling channel after the 2022 return to in person education.
objectives: Guarantee continuity of the school year during COVID-19 school closures
Reach students across the digital divide by combining web, television and radio delivery
Provide content aligned with the national curriculum, including in indigenous languages and for students with disabilities
Support teachers and families in accompanying remote learning
mechanisms: The ministry produced weekly learning sessions aligned with the national curriculum and broadcast them on the state television channel and a network of radio stations, while a web platform hosted guided activities by grade. Private telecom operators zero rated the platform, and teachers followed up with students by phone and WhatsApp, adapting and complementing the broadcast content. Radio programming was produced in several indigenous languages, and complementary tablet distribution targeted students without connectivity.
coverage: Ministry figures from 2020 indicate that over 85 to 90 percent of Peru's roughly 8 million basic education students connected with the strategy through at least one channel.
impactSummary: There is no rigorous impact evaluation of effects on learning. Evidence is mainly descriptive, including a large phone survey of about 8,000 households by Innovations for Poverty Action documenting high but unequal engagement, with access and participation gaps by region, income and connectivity, and ministry monitoring data on reach and satisfaction. Studies of the pandemic period in Peru document substantial learning losses despite the strategy, but these cannot be attributed causally to the program design.

name: Millennium Schools
summaryShort: A flagship school infrastructure program of the Correa government that built large, fully equipped public schools in poor and rural areas of Ecuador from 2008; construction was halted after 2017 but existing schools continue to operate.
summaryLong: The Unidades Educativas del Milenio were conceived in 2007 and inaugurated from 2008 as model public schools with laboratories, computer and language facilities, libraries and modern buildings, intended to bring high quality educational services to historically underserved areas. Spatial analyses found that the large majority of UEMs were located in areas of extreme poverty. By 2017 around 100 to 117 UEMs had been built at a reported cost of roughly 800 million dollars, serving over 83,000 students, while the policy was accompanied by the closure or consolidation of many small rural schools. A 2015 contract with a Chinese company to add 200 prefabricated UEMs was terminated by the Moreno government in 2018, and new construction stopped, although the existing schools remain part of the public system.
objectives: Improve the quality of public education infrastructure in poor and rural areas
Expand access to complete basic and secondary education with laboratories and technology
Serve historically excluded populations, including indigenous communities
Act as reference schools for surrounding educational institutions
mechanisms: The Ministry of Education selected sites prioritizing poverty and unmet demand, built large standardized campuses with classrooms, science and computer laboratories and other facilities, and staffed and equipped them as regular public schools, often replacing or consolidating dispersed small rural schools whose students were transferred to the new units. Each UEM was expected to anchor a network of nearby schools.
coverage: Around 117 schools built by 2017 serving 83,425 students, with an investment estimated at about 803 million dollars.
impactSummary: An IDB financed quasi-experimental evaluation by FLACSO Ecuador using 2015 and 2016 data found a large positive impact on mathematics achievement of about 0.5 standard deviations for students attending UEMs, no measurable impact on language achievement, and no impact on enrollment. Critics and qualitative studies argue the schools were costly, displaced community and intercultural bilingual schools, and increased travel distances for some rural students.

name: New School
summaryShort: A rural multigrade schooling model developed in Colombia in the mid 1970s by Vicky Colbert, Oscar Mogollón and Beryl Levinger that combines self paced learning guides, active pedagogy, flexible promotion and community participation; it became national rural policy in the 1980s and has been replicated internationally.
summaryLong: Escuela Nueva emerged in 1975 as an improvement on Colombia's one teacher rural unitary schools, formalizing a model in which one or two teachers manage several grades simultaneously using structured self instructional learning guides, student government, classroom learning corners, flexible promotion and strong community involvement. With support from the Coffee Growers Federation, the Inter-American Development Bank and later the World Bank, the program expanded from pilot schools to roughly 8,000 schools by 1986 and was then scaled as national policy toward some 20,000 rural schools. The model has been adapted in numerous countries and is sustained in Colombia by the Ministry of Education and by the Fundación Escuela Nueva Volvamos a la Gente, founded by Vicky Colbert, whose work has received international recognition including the Yidan Prize.
objectives: Provide complete, quality primary education in low density rural areas through multigrade teaching
Replace rote teaching with active, student centered and cooperative learning
Reduce repetition and dropout through flexible promotion adapted to rural life
Strengthen ties between school, family and community
mechanisms: Teachers in multigrade rural schools use sequenced self instructional learning guides that let students advance at their own pace individually or in small groups, while the teacher acts as facilitator across grades. Classrooms are organized with learning corners and small libraries, students participate in school government to build civic skills, promotion between grades is flexible so that children who miss time for harvests can resume without repeating, and teachers are trained through workshops and peer microcenters. Community members participate in school activities and management.
coverage: Expanded to about 8,000 schools by 1986 and to roughly 20,000 rural schools with World Bank support thereafter, reaching hundreds of thousands of Colombian rural students; the model has since been adapted in more than a dozen countries.
impactSummary: Multiple peer reviewed quasi-experimental studies from the late 1980s and 1990s found that Escuela Nueva students outperformed students in conventional rural schools in third grade Spanish and mathematics and in fifth grade Spanish, and scored higher on civic values and self esteem measures, with evidence of lower dropout. Effects vary across samples and the studies are observational, so selection into the program cannot be fully ruled out. The model is widely cited as one of the most successful rural education innovations in the developing world.

name: Everyone Learning Program
summaryShort: Colombia's largest in service teacher professional development program, launched by the Ministry of National Education in 2011 and implemented from 2012, in which trained tutors coach primary school teachers in low performing public schools and distribute structured teaching materials.
summaryLong: The Programa Todos a Aprender, formally the program for the transformation of educational quality, was launched in 2011 and has operated since 2012 as the Colombian government's main instrument to raise learning in primary education in public schools with weak results, a majority of them rural. The program selects and trains a cadre of expert teachers who work as tutors, each accompanying teachers in a set of focused schools through classroom observation, feedback, and situated training sessions, complemented by the mass distribution of textbooks and teacher guides in mathematics and language. The program was relaunched as PTA 2.0 in 2015 and has continued under successive governments, with national coverage figures around 4,000 to 4,500 school establishments and roughly 84,000 to 100,000 teachers accompanied in recent cycles.
objectives: Improve learning outcomes in mathematics and language in primary grades of low performing public schools
Transform classroom practice through situated professional development and coaching by tutors
Provide high quality textbooks and teacher guides at scale
Close urban rural gaps in educational quality
mechanisms: The ministry identifies low performing public schools using national Saber test results and assigns each a tutor, an outstanding teacher selected by competition and trained by a smaller group of trainers. Tutors visit schools regularly, model and observe lessons, give feedback, and run study communities of teachers, following a structured pedagogical route. Schools receive student textbooks and teacher guides aligned with national standards in mathematics and language, and program operation is monitored through cycles of accompaniment.
coverage: In 2020 the program operated in 798 municipalities and about 4,500 school establishments covering more than 14,000 school sites, accompanying over 83,000 classroom teachers with about 4,400 tutors; by September 2021 it had accompanied 100,794 teachers.

name: Canaima Educational Project
summaryShort: Venezuela's one laptop per child style program, launched in 2009, which has distributed millions of small laptops known as Canaimitas with free software and curricular content to public school students, later extended to secondary and with tablets to other levels.
summaryLong: Canaima Educativo began in 2009 under the government of Hugo Chávez as a program to deliver portable computers loaded with educational content to students and teachers in public and subsidized primary schools, using the Venezuelan Canaima GNU Linux operating system and locally developed digital content. The program started with classroom use in first grade and moved to a model in which children take the Canaimita home, and from 2013 it was extended to secondary education students. Government sources report cumulative deliveries rising from about 2.35 million devices in the early 2010s to more than 6 million laptops and tablets by 2017, with reported state investment of around 600 million dollars between 2013 and 2016. Deliveries have continued intermittently in subsequent years amid Venezuela's economic crisis.

Support the national curriculum with locally produced free software and digital resources
Promote technological sovereignty through the Canaima GNU Linux platform and local assembly
Reduce the digital divide for low income students and their families

Devices are distributed free of charge through public and subsidized schools, first for in classroom use in early grades and then under home use schemes, with teachers also receiving equipment and some training. Content updates and maintenance run through state technology agencies, and the scheme was later broadened with tablets for secondary and university students.
coverage: Government figures report more than 6 million devices delivered between 2009 and 2017, including about 4.5 million reported by 2014, with roughly 600 million dollars invested between 2013 and 2016.

name: Education with Community Participation
nameLocal: Programa de Educación con Participación de la Comunidad
summaryShort: A post civil war program that expanded preschool and basic education in rural El Salvador by transferring school management, including teacher hiring and firing, to elected parent associations (ACEs). It became one of the most internationally cited community-managed schooling models before being phased out after 2009.
summaryLong:
EDUCO was launched in 1991, as El Salvador emerged from civil war, with World Bank support, to rapidly expand education in poor rural areas where the state had little presence. Communities formed legally recognized Community Education Associations (Asociaciones Comunales para la Educación, ACEs), groups of five volunteer parents with legal status and financial authority, which signed agreements with the Ministry of Education, received public funds, and hired, paid, and could dismiss teachers on annual contracts. Initially limited to preschool and grades 1 to 3, the program was extended to grade 6 in 1994 and to grade 9 in 1997.

By 2010, around 55 percent of rural public schools, equivalent to roughly a third of all schools in El Salvador, operated under EDUCO. The program attracted intense international attention as a model of school-based management, but it was also criticized for relying on precarious teacher contracts. After the FMLN government took office in 2009 the program was wound down, and in 2011 some 8,472 EDUCO teachers were absorbed into regular Ministry of Education positions.
objectives: Rapidly expand access to preschool and basic education in poor rural communities after the civil war
Decentralize school management to parent associations to increase accountability of teachers to communities
Reduce student absenteeism and teacher absenteeism through local monitoring
Strengthen community participation in public service delivery
mechanisms: The Ministry of Education transferred public funds directly to elected, legally constituted parent associations (ACEs) in each community. The ACE hired teachers on renewable one-year contracts, paid salaries, purchased materials, and monitored attendance, while the ministry set the curriculum, provided training, and supervised the agreements. Teacher accountability to parents, rather than to the central ministry, was the core incentive mechanism.
coverage: By 2010 about 55 percent of rural public schools (roughly one third of all schools in El Salvador) operated under EDUCO; 8,472 EDUCO teachers were transferred to ministry payroll positions in 2011 when the program closed.
impactSummary: The best known evaluation, by Jimenez and Sawada (1999), used selection-corrected models on standardized tests and found that EDUCO schools improved students' language scores and reduced student absences relative to traditional schools, with no deficit in math. Later panel work by the same authors suggested community management helped retain students. However, subsequent academic critiques argued the measured achievement advantages were small and sensitive to specification, so the evidence is best read as moderate rather than definitive.

name: National Program of Self-Management for Educational Development
nameLocal: Programa Nacional de Autogestión para el Desarrollo Educativo
summaryShort: Guatemala's community-managed schools program, formalized in 1996 after the Peace Accords, funded parent committees (COEDUCAs) to run schools in remote, mostly indigenous communities. It grew to more than 4,600 schools and over 445,000 children before being dismantled from 2008.
summaryLong:
PRONADE grew out of pilot efforts begun in the early 1990s and was formally established by Governmental Agreement 457-96 in 1996, the year Guatemala signed its Peace Accords, which committed the state to expanding rural education. Communities at least three kilometers from the nearest government school, with at least 25 primary-age children and no teachers already on the public payroll, formed Education Committees (Comités Educativos, COEDUCAs) that received funds directly from the Ministry of Education to hire, pay, and dismiss teachers, set the school calendar, and buy materials and school snacks. Contracted NGOs (ISEs) supported and monitored the committees instead of the regular ministry bureaucracy.

The program expanded from 19 pilot communities in Chimaltenango to more than 4,631 schools serving over 445,000 pre-primary and primary children, concentrated in rural indigenous areas. Primary enrollment in Guatemala rose about 26 percent between 1996 and 2000, and roughly half of that increase came through PRONADE. The model was praised for expanding access cheaply but criticized by teacher unions over precarious contracts and by researchers over quality. Following a campaign promise by President Álvaro Colom, the government dismantled PRONADE starting in 2008 and transferred its teachers into the regular system.
objectives: Expand education coverage in remote rural and indigenous communities not reached by the traditional system
Transfer school management and teacher hiring to organized parent committees
Increase enrollment quickly and at low cost in line with the 1996 Peace Accords
Foster community participation and local accountability in education
mechanisms: The Ministry of Education transferred public funds directly to legally constituted community education committees (COEDUCAs), which hired and paid teachers, set calendars, and purchased materials and school snacks. Contracted NGOs, called Instituciones de Servicios Educativos, organized and trained the committees and handled administration. Eligibility rules targeted communities far from existing schools, ensuring the program reached previously unserved populations.
coverage: More than 4,631 community schools and over 445,000 pre-primary and primary students by the mid 2000s; about half of Guatemala's 26 percent primary enrollment increase between 1996 and 2000 came through PRONADE.
impactSummary: PRONADE clearly expanded access in hard-to-reach communities, and World Bank comparative work on Central American school-based management found its schools maximized community participation while operating with less experienced teachers and fewer inputs. However, the program never received a rigorous experimental or strong quasi-experimental impact evaluation of learning outcomes, so evidence on quality effects is limited to descriptive and comparative studies.

name: Honduran Community Education Program
summaryShort: Community-managed schools program created in 1999 after Hurricane Mitch to bring pre-basic and basic education to isolated rural Honduran communities, with parent associations hiring and supervising teachers. It still operates under the Secretariat of Education.
summaryLong:
PROHECO was created in 1999, in the aftermath of Hurricane Mitch, to expand schooling in isolated rural areas where roughly a quarter of rural school-age children lacked access to primary education in the late 1990s. Modeled on El Salvador's EDUCO, it channels public funds to community education associations (AECOs) made up of parents, which hire, pay, and monitor teachers and manage day-to-day school operations, while the Secretariat of Education provides curriculum, training, and oversight.

By the mid 2000s the program had created more than 3,000 schools accounting for roughly 8 percent of total primary enrollment. PROHECO teachers work on community contracts outside the teacher unions, which insulated the schools from strikes but also drew criticism over job security and teacher qualifications. The program continues to operate as the Secretariat of Education's alternative delivery model for remote communities, including indigenous and Afro-Honduran populations.
objectives: Expand access to pre-basic and basic education in isolated rural communities
Involve parents directly in school management and teacher supervision
Rebuild and extend education services in areas affected by Hurricane Mitch
Reach indigenous and Afro-Honduran communities underserved by the traditional system
mechanisms: Communities form legally recognized parent associations (AECOs) that receive government transfers to hire and pay teachers on annual contracts, manage small budgets, and oversee attendance and school upkeep. The Secretariat of Education sets the curriculum, trains teachers and associations, and supervises through departmental promoters. Teacher accountability to the local association, rather than to the central ministry or unions, is the core design feature.
coverage: More than 3,000 community schools and roughly 8 percent of total primary enrollment by the mid 2000s; the program continues to operate nationally in rural areas (Secretariat of Education).
impactSummary: A quasi-experimental study by Di Gropello and Marshall using standardized tests in 120 rural schools found PROHECO schools achieved higher science scores than comparable traditional rural schools, with no significant differences in math or language. The study found PROHECO increased teacher effort and parental involvement, but these advantages were partly offset by less experienced, less trained teachers and smaller classes. There is no experimental evidence, and effects on enrollment have not been rigorously isolated.

keyOutcomes.effect: Positive and significant relative to comparable traditional rural schools

name: School Autonomy Reform (Autonomous Schools Program)
summaryShort: One of the most radical school-based management experiments in the world: from 1993 Nicaragua transferred budget and personnel decisions to school councils with parent majorities, partly financed by fees charged to families. The model was abolished in January 2007 when the incoming government decreed education free.
summaryLong:
Beginning in 1993, Nicaragua's Ministry of Education converted public schools into autonomous schools governed by local school councils (consejos directivos) in which parents held a voting majority. Councils could hire and dismiss directors and teachers, manage budgets based on per-student transfers, and raise additional revenue, in part through fees charged to parents. The reform expanded quickly: within three years about 100 secondary schools and more than 200 primary schools had entered the regime, and the model continued to spread through the late 1990s and early 2000s with support from the World Bank and other donors, becoming the country's dominant school governance model.

The reform was studied intensively by World Bank researchers, who distinguished between de jure autonomy (formal status) and de facto autonomy (actual local decision-making). The fee component proved controversial because it shifted costs to poor families. In January 2007, immediately after taking office, the Ortega government declared public education free again and abolished the autonomy regime, recentralizing school management.
objectives: Decentralize school management decisions to councils dominated by parents
Increase school-level accountability for personnel and budget decisions
Mobilize local resources for schools through per-student transfers and fees
Improve learning outcomes through local decision-making
mechanisms: Participating schools signed contracts with the Ministry of Education creating directive councils with parent majorities. Councils received monthly per-student fiscal transfers, controlled school budgets, could hire and fire the school director and teachers, and could charge and retain fees from families. The ministry retained curriculum and standards while shifting operational authority to schools.
coverage: About 100 secondary schools and more than 200 primary schools entered the regime within the first three years (King et al. 1996); the model continued expanding through the late 1990s and early 2000s to cover a large share of public schools before being abolished in January 2007.
impactSummary: World Bank evaluations by King and Ozler found that formal (de jure) autonomy by itself had no clear effect on achievement, but greater de facto autonomy, that is, actual local influence over staffing and pedagogy, was associated with better student test performance. Later case study work documented wide variation in how councils functioned and raised equity concerns about fees. No experimental evidence exists, and the reform was abolished for political and equity reasons rather than on the basis of evaluation results.

keyOutcomes.effect: Greater de facto school-level decision-making was associated with higher student test scores; formal autonomous status alone showed no clear effect

name: Social Protection Network
summaryShort: Nicaragua's PROGRESA-style conditional cash transfer (2000-2006), randomized at the community level, paid poor rural households cash conditional on primary school enrollment and health checkups. One of the most rigorously evaluated CCTs in the world, it ended in 2006 despite strong results.
summaryLong:
Launched in 2000 with Inter-American Development Bank financing and modeled on Mexico's PROGRESA, the Red de Protección Social gave poor rural households bimonthly cash transfers conditional on enrolling children aged 7 to 13 who had not completed fourth grade in primary school, maintaining attendance, and taking young children to preventive health appointments. A pilot phase (2000-2002) covered around 10,000 households and a second phase (2002-2006) covered about 30,000 households.

Because the pilot was randomized across 42 rural comarcas, RPS produced some of the strongest evidence in the CCT literature. IFPRI's evaluation found large gains in enrollment, attendance, and grade progression, concentrated among the poorest households, alongside improved child nutrition. Follow-up studies a decade later found lasting gains in schooling, learning, and earnings for boys who were exposed at the right ages. Despite this record, the program was discontinued in 2006 amid weak domestic political support, making RPS a frequently cited case of an effective but short-lived program.
objectives: Increase primary school enrollment, attendance, and grade progression among poor rural children
Reduce child labor among school-age children
Improve health and nutrition of children under five
Supplement income of extremely poor rural households to reduce current and future poverty
mechanisms: Eligible households in targeted poor rural communities received a food security transfer plus a school attendance transfer and a per-child school supplies transfer, paid every two months to the female caregiver. Education transfers were conditional on enrollment and regular attendance of children aged 7 to 13 who had not completed fourth grade; health transfers were conditional on preventive checkups for young children. Noncompliance led to suspension of payments.
coverage: About 10,000 households in the randomized pilot phase (2000-2002) and roughly 30,000 households in the expanded second phase (2002-2006) in poor rural areas of central and northern Nicaragua (CEPAL program database; Moore 2009).
impactSummary: The randomized IFPRI evaluation found large positive double-difference effects on school enrollment, attendance, and grade advancement, with the biggest gains among the extremely poor, plus reductions in child labor and improvements in child nutrition. Ten-year follow-up studies exploiting the randomized phase-in found persistent gains of roughly half a grade of completed schooling and significant learning and earnings gains for young men exposed at primary school age, demonstrating that CCT effects can outlast the program itself.

name: Family Allowance Program
summaryShort: Honduras' first large cash transfer program (1990) whose second phase, PRAF-II (2000-2005), gave education and health vouchers to poor rural households conditional on primary enrollment and health visits, evaluated through a municipality-level randomized experiment. It was succeeded by Bono 10,000 in 2010.
summaryLong:
PRAF was created in 1990 as a compensatory social program. Its internationally known phase, PRAF-II, ran from 2000 to 2005 with Inter-American Development Bank support and delivered two kinds of transfers in poor rural municipalities: demand-side cash vouchers to households, conditional on enrolling children aged 6 to 12 who had not completed fourth grade and on regular health center visits for young children, and supply-side transfers to parent associations and local health teams to strengthen schools and clinics.

In October 1999, before rollout, researchers randomly assigned 70 of the poorest municipalities, ranked by child height-for-age, into demand-side, supply-side, combined, and control groups, with 40 municipalities receiving the household transfers. This design made PRAF one of the few CCTs in the world evaluated through a true randomized experiment at scale. Evaluations found significant enrollment gains and reductions in child labor, though transfer values were small relative to other CCTs. PRAF transfers were replaced in 2010 by the larger Bono 10,000 program.
objectives: Increase primary school enrollment and attendance among poor rural children aged 6 to 12
Reduce child labor
Increase use of preventive maternal and child health services
Strengthen local school and health service supply through transfers to parent associations and health teams
mechanisms: Eligible households in randomly selected poor municipalities received education vouchers for each child aged 6 to 12 who had not completed fourth grade, conditional on enrollment and attendance, plus health vouchers conditional on health center visits for young children and pregnant women. A parallel supply-side arm transferred resources to parent associations and primary health teams. Payments were modest and delivered semiannually.
coverage: PRAF-II operated in 50 of the 70 poorest municipalities of western Honduras under the experimental design (40 with household transfers), reaching tens of thousands of poor rural households between 2000 and 2005.
impactSummary: Randomized evaluations found that the demand-side transfers increased primary school enrollment, with Glewwe and Olinto (2004) estimating enrollment about 7 percentage points higher in treated municipalities in 2001, and J-PAL summaries of Galiani and McEwan's analysis reporting enrollment gains of about 12 percent and reductions of roughly 30 percent in child work outside the home among eligible children. Galiani and McEwan (2013) showed effects were strongly concentrated in the poorest municipalities and households. Long-term follow-up by Molina Millán and coauthors found lasting effects on secondary completion and higher education among exposed cohorts. Supply-side transfers showed weaker effects, partly due to implementation problems.

name: Avancemos Conditional Cash Transfer Program
summaryShort: Costa Rica's national conditional cash transfer, created in 2006, pays monthly subsidies to poor families so adolescents stay in school instead of working. Administered by IMAS, it reached about 274,000 students in 2023 and was given a permanent legal basis by Law 9617.
summaryLong:
Avancemos was established on 8 May 2006 to reduce secondary school dropout among adolescents from families in poverty, on the premise that a monetary subsidy conditional on school attendance offsets the opportunity cost of adolescent work. The program is administered by the Instituto Mixto de Ayuda Social (IMAS), with beneficiaries selected through the national social registry (SINIRUBE), and is coordinated with the Ministry of Public Education and the Ministry of Labor. Law No. 9617 of 2018 strengthened the program's legal foundation.

Transfers are paid monthly to families conditional on enrollment and permanence in the education system. In 2023 amounts were 18,000 colones per month for primary students and 30,000 to 40,000 colones for secondary students depending on grade, and the government programmed transfers for about 274,000 students. Originally focused on secondary students, the conditional transfer scheme now also covers students in primary education under the IMAS benefit structure. Several quasi-experimental evaluations have found positive effects on attendance, permanence, and reinsertion of dropouts.
objectives: Reduce dropout and promote permanence in secondary education among adolescents in poverty
Offset the opportunity cost of adolescent labor through a monthly cash subsidy
Promote reinsertion of out-of-school youth into the education system
Link poor families to the social protection system through the national beneficiary registry
mechanisms: IMAS pays a monthly cash transfer to eligible families identified through the SINIRUBE social registry, conditional on the student's enrollment, attendance, and permanence in primary or secondary education. Amounts increase with education level (18,000 colones for primary, 30,000 for lower secondary, 40,000 for upper secondary per month in 2023). Noncompliance with study conditions leads to suspension of the benefit.
coverage: About 274,000 students programmed to receive transfers in 2023 (Government of Costa Rica / IMAS); the program operates nationwide and is targeted to households in poverty or extreme poverty.
impactSummary: Quasi-experimental evaluations using propensity score matching and difference-in-differences designs have found that Avancemos reduced dropout and promoted reinsertion, with estimates that 10 to 16 percent of beneficiary students who stayed in school did so because of the program, and analyses of national household survey data finding higher attendance and educational attainment along with a lower probability of adolescent work. There is no experimental evidence, and estimates vary across methods and periods.

keyOutcomes.effect: Between 10 and 16 percent of beneficiary students who did not leave high school stayed only because of Avancemos, per quasi-experimental estimates
Higher school attendance and additional years of attainment, with a lower probability of adolescent work, in household survey analyses for 2006-2014

name: National Bilingual Education Program (now Bilingual Intercultural Education)
summaryShort: Guatemala's flagship Mayan-Spanish bilingual education policy, created as PRONEBI in 1984 and later institutionalized in the Ministry of Education as the Directorate General of Bilingual Intercultural Education (DIGEBI), delivering early primary instruction in Mayan languages alongside Spanish.
summaryLong:
PRONEBI was established by Government Accord No. 1093-84 in 1984, building on a 1980-1984 USAID-supported pilot project, to provide bilingual preschool and early primary education to rural indigenous children. Its first five years were financed by a USAID loan of 10.2 million dollars and a 3.3 million dollar grant plus 25 million dollars from the Guatemalan government. The program initially targeted 800 schools, 400 complete schools offering a preschool through fourth grade bilingual curriculum and 400 incomplete schools offering bilingual preschool, in the four largest Mayan language communities: K'iche', Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi' and Mam.

In the mid 1990s the program was institutionalized inside the Ministry of Education as the Directorate General of Bilingual Intercultural Education (DIGEBI), and after the 1996 Peace Accords bilingual intercultural education became a formal state commitment. By 2005 bilingual programs had expanded to cover 12 language communities, including Garifuna and Xinka. Coverage and quality remain uneven relative to the size of Guatemala's indigenous school-age population, and the policy has been analyzed mainly through non-experimental studies.
objectives: Provide initial literacy and early primary instruction in children's Mayan mother tongue alongside Spanish
Reduce grade repetition and dropout among rural indigenous students
Improve learning outcomes including Spanish acquisition
Preserve and promote Mayan languages and cultures within the public school system
mechanisms: The ministry develops bilingual curricula and teaching materials in Mayan languages, recruits and trains bilingual indigenous teachers, and designates bilingual schools in indigenous municipalities. Instruction begins in the mother tongue in preschool and early grades with Spanish introduced progressively, transitioning toward bilingual instruction by the end of early primary. Since the mid 1990s DIGEBI administers the model nationally.
coverage: Initial target of 800 rural schools in the four major Mayan language groups (K'iche', Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi', Mam) in the 1980s; expanded to programs in 12 language communities by 2005 under DIGEBI.
impactSummary: Non-experimental analyses using 1986-1991 program data found that students in PRONEBI bilingual schools had higher attendance and promotion rates, lower repetition and dropout, and higher test scores across subjects including Spanish, and World Bank simulations suggested the program could pay for itself through reduced repetition costs. However, the evidence base rests on descriptive comparisons rather than rigorous causal designs, and no experimental evaluation of the policy exists.

keyOutcomes.effect: Bilingual school students showed lower grade repetition and dropout rates than comparable indigenous students in Spanish-only schools, with simulated cost savings from reduced repetition

evaluations.keyFinding: Students in bilingual schools had higher attendance and promotion and lower repetition and dropout, and projected savings from reduced repetition exceeded program costs.

name: Bilingual Panama Program
summaryShort: Panama's national English teaching initiative, launched in 2014 and made law in 2017, that trains public school English teachers, including immersion stays abroad, and expands English instruction for primary and secondary students in official schools.
summaryLong:
Panamá Bilingüe was launched in 2014 by the incoming Varela administration as an emergency effort to improve English teaching in public schools, motivated by Panama's weak English proficiency rankings despite its service-oriented economy. The program, run centrally by the Ministry of Education (MEDUCA), combines in-country teacher training, immersion scholarships that send public school teachers to universities in the United States, the United Kingdom and other English-speaking countries (with an initial goal of about 500 teachers per year), and expanded English instruction for primary (Kids) and secondary (After School) students. Government targets called for reaching about 285,000 students and training 25,000 teachers, at a pace of roughly 2,000 teachers per year.

Law 18 of 10 May 2017 gave the program permanent legal status and created the National Directorate of Foreign Language Teaching within MEDUCA to plan, coordinate, and evaluate bilingual education nationwide. The program has continued under subsequent administrations as the basis of Panama's state English policy. No rigorous impact evaluation of its effects on student learning has been published; available studies are qualitative analyses of the teacher training components.
objectives: Improve English proficiency of students in official public schools
Train and certify Panamanian English teachers, including through immersion programs abroad
Institutionalize English as a second language teaching in the public system through a permanent national directorate
Strengthen graduates' competitiveness and labor market insertion in Panama's service economy
mechanisms: MEDUCA selects in-service and pre-service English teachers for training, including eight-week or longer immersion stays at partner universities abroad and in-country professional development, and deploys expanded English instruction blocks for primary students (Kids component) and secondary students (After School component). Law 18 of 2017 created the National Directorate of Foreign Language Teaching to coordinate, supervise, and evaluate the program and required teacher certification.
coverage: Design targets of about 285,000 students reached and 25,000 teachers trained over five years, with roughly 2,000 teachers trained per year and about 500 teachers per year sent abroad during the initial phase (MEDUCA and partner university reports).
impactSummary: The program has not been rigorously evaluated. No experimental or quasi-experimental study of its effects on student English proficiency or other learning outcomes has been published. Available evidence consists of qualitative studies of the study-abroad teacher training component, which report that teachers valued immersion and learned new techniques but found the training imperfectly matched to Panamanian classroom conditions, where low primary teacher proficiency and inadequate facilities remain obstacles.

name: Full-Time Schools Program
summaryShort: Federal program that extended the school day in public basic education schools from 4.5 to 6 or 8 hours, with food services in the most marginalized communities. It operated from 2007 until its cancellation in February 2022.
summaryLong: The Programa Escuelas de Tiempo Completo was launched by Mexico's Secretariat of Public Education in 2007 to lengthen the school day in public basic education schools, adding time for academics, arts, physical activity, and, in marginalized areas, school meals. By the late 2010s more than 25,000 schools had joined and the program reached roughly 3.6 million students, with priority given to schools in high-poverty and indigenous communities. On February 28, 2022 the federal government eliminated the program when it published the 2022 operating rules of La Escuela es Nuestra, a decision widely criticized because rigorous studies had documented learning gains and benefits for working mothers.
objectives: Extend instructional time in public primary and basic education schools
Improve learning outcomes in math and reading, especially in marginalized communities
Provide food services in schools serving high-poverty populations
Support working parents, particularly mothers, by lengthening the time children spend in school
mechanisms: Participating public schools extended their daily schedule from 4.5 hours to 6 or 8 hours. The federal government transferred resources to states to pay salary supplements to teachers and principals for the additional hours, fund pedagogical materials, and, in schools in high-marginalization areas, finance food services. Schools entered the program gradually, and the staggered adoption across schools and years is what later allowed quasi-experimental evaluation.
coverage: More than 25,000 public basic education schools and roughly 3.6 million students at its peak before cancellation in 2022, up from fewer than 500 schools in 2007.
impactSummary: Multiple published quasi-experimental studies find positive effects. Extending the school day improved math and reading test scores, with effects growing over time and larger gains in high-poverty schools, and it had long-lasting effects on high-stakes high school admission scores, especially for girls. It also increased mothers' labor force participation and reduced child labor.

name: The School is Ours
summaryShort: Flagship federal program since 2019 that transfers cash grants directly to parent-led school committees to fund infrastructure, maintenance, and equipment in public basic education schools, prioritizing marginalized and indigenous communities.
summaryLong: La Escuela es Nuestra was launched in October 2019 by the government of President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador as its main school infrastructure program. It delivers grants directly to school assemblies and committees of parents (Comites Escolares de Administracion Participativa), bypassing intermediaries, so that communities themselves decide and execute spending on construction, maintenance, and equipment. After the 2022 cancellation of the Full-Time Schools Program, LEEN absorbed components for extended hours and food services in some schools. Federal audits by the Auditoria Superior de la Federacion have criticized weak documentation, monitoring, and evaluation mechanisms, and the program has no rigorous impact evaluation.
objectives: Improve the physical infrastructure and equipment of public basic education schools
Channel federal resources directly to school communities without intermediaries
Prioritize schools in highly marginalized, rural, and indigenous localities
Strengthen parent and community participation in school management
mechanisms: Schools form a participatory administration committee composed of parents and community members. The federal government deposits a grant, originally at least 150,000 pesos per school depending on enrollment size, directly into a committee account. The committee decides spending priorities, contracts works, and reports back to the school assembly. Since 2022 some schools can also use funds for extended schedules and food services, components inherited from the cancelled Full-Time Schools Program.
coverage: Since 2019 the program has provided 404,588 grants to more than 187,000 public schools according to Education Ministry data reported in 2026, with a planned investment of 113 billion pesos for the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
impactSummary: No rigorous impact evaluation exists. Evidence is limited to government diagnostics and federal audit reports. The Auditoria Superior de la Federacion found that the education ministry could not document works completed in most beneficiary schools in 2021, and observers note the operating rules lack monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, so effects on learning or infrastructure quality are unknown.

name: 2013 Education Reform and Professional Teacher Service
nameLocal: Reforma Educativa de 2013 y Servicio Profesional Docente
summaryShort: Constitutional reform that created a merit-based teacher career system (Servicio Profesional Docente) with compulsory evaluations and gave constitutional autonomy to the evaluation institute INEE. It was repealed in 2019.
summaryLong: The 2013 education reform under President Enrique Pena Nieto amended the constitution to establish that teacher hiring, promotion, and permanence in public basic and upper secondary education would be governed by competitive, exam-based processes under the new Servicio Profesional Docente, ending discretionary and union-mediated allocation of teaching posts. The reform granted constitutional autonomy to the Instituto Nacional para la Evaluacion de la Educacion (INEE), which designed and oversaw mandatory teacher performance evaluations; incumbent teachers who failed the evaluation three times could be removed from classroom duties. The reform faced intense opposition from dissident teacher unions. In 2019 the government of President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador repealed it, eliminated the INEE, replaced it with the commission MEJOREDU, and removed performance evaluation as a condition for job permanence, with the new legal framework in effect from September 2019.
objectives: Establish merit-based, exam-driven rules for teacher hiring, promotion, and permanence
Reduce union and political discretion in the allocation of teaching posts
Create an autonomous national institute (INEE) to evaluate teachers, schools, and the education system
Improve teaching quality and student learning in basic and upper secondary education
mechanisms: The reform amended Article 3 of the constitution and created secondary legislation (Ley General del Servicio Profesional Docente and Ley del INEE). New teachers had to win posts through national competitive examinations, promotions to leadership positions required exams, and incumbent teachers underwent compulsory performance evaluations designed by the INEE, with training support and consequences for repeated failure. A national coordination office of the SPD organized hiring pools with states.
coverage: Applied nationwide to public basic and upper secondary education; over its six years of operation the SPD subjected hundreds of thousands of teaching post assignments and promotions to competitive examination across all 32 states.
impactSummary: Quasi-experimental evidence indicates that exam-based, rule-driven teacher hiring of the kind universalized by the reform selected more effective teachers than discretionary hiring. A World Bank study of the 2013 reform finds that rule-based recruitment improved the quality of new hires as measured by student learning. System-wide effects are harder to attribute because the reform was repealed after six years.

name: Telesecundaria Televised Lower Secondary Schools
summaryShort: A nationwide system of lower secondary schools, created in 1968, in which lessons are delivered through televised broadcasts supported by a single classroom teacher, allowing junior secondary education to reach small rural communities.
summaryLong: Telesecundaria was created by the Mexican government in 1968 to expand access to lower secondary education in rural communities that could not attract subject-specialist teachers. In a telesecundaria, students in each grade receive lessons across all subjects through televised programs produced centrally, while one generalist teacher per grade facilitates learning, with the same instructional hours (30 per week, 200 days per year) as conventional schools. The model expanded massively from the 1990s with satellite delivery and remains a core part of the Mexican system, serving about 1.5 million students, roughly a fifth of total lower secondary enrollment. It is one of the world's largest and longest-running distance education programs and has inspired similar models in Central America.
objectives: Expand access to lower secondary education in small rural localities
Overcome the shortage of subject-specialist teachers outside cities
Reduce urban-rural gaps in educational attainment
Deliver a standardized national curriculum at low cost through television
mechanisms: Centrally produced televised lessons, originally broadcast live and later distributed by satellite (EDUSAT) and digital media, cover the full lower secondary curriculum. Each school operates with one teacher per grade who guides students through the televised segments, accompanying workbooks, and assessments. Because a telesecundaria requires fewer specialized staff, schools can operate in localities too small for conventional secondary schools.
coverage: About 1.5 million students, roughly 20 percent of Mexico's lower secondary enrollment, across more than 18,000 schools concentrated in rural areas (late 2010s and early 2020s).
impactSummary: Several rigorous studies find large positive effects. Expansion of telesecundarias increased junior secondary enrollment and years of schooling, raised adult incomes, and shifted workers out of agriculture and informality. Recent structural and quasi-experimental work finds students gain significantly in math and Spanish relative to traditional schools, with effects strongest for students in remote areas.

name: Basic Education Financing Funds (FUNDEF and FUNDEB)
nameLocal: Fundo de Manutencao e Desenvolvimento da Educacao Basica e de Valorizacao dos Profissionais da Educacao
summaryShort: Brazil's constitutional education financing mechanism, created as FUNDEF in 1996, expanded into FUNDEB in 2006-2007, and made permanent in 2020, which pools state and municipal tax revenue and redistributes it per student, with federal top-ups for the poorest networks.
summaryLong: FUNDEF (Fundo de Manutencao e Desenvolvimento do Ensino Fundamental e de Valorizacao do Magisterio) was created by constitutional amendment in 1996 and implemented nationally in 1998. It earmarked a share of state and municipal tax revenues into state-level funds redistributed in proportion to primary school enrollment, with a federal complement where per-student values fell below a national minimum, and required that at least 60 percent of resources pay teacher salaries. In 2006-2007 it was replaced by FUNDEB, which extended the mechanism to all of basic education from early childhood to upper secondary. Constitutional Amendment 108 of August 2020 made FUNDEB permanent and raised the federal complement gradually from 10 percent to 23 percent of the funds by 2026, with new equity-based distribution criteria (VAAF, VAAT, and VAAR) and priority resources for early childhood education.
objectives: Equalize per-student spending across states and municipalities
Guarantee a national minimum level of funding for every basic education student
Raise and protect teacher pay, with a fixed share of resources earmarked for educators
Increase enrollment and completion in basic education, especially in poor regions
mechanisms: A constitutionally fixed share (20 percent under FUNDEB) of designated state and municipal taxes is pooled into a fund within each state and redistributed to state and municipal school networks in proportion to enrollment, weighted by education level and modality. The federal government tops up funds in states that cannot reach the national minimum per-student value; under the 2020 reform, additional federal complements reward networks that reduce inequality and improve learning. At least 70 percent of FUNDEB resources must be spent on the remuneration of education professionals.
coverage: Covers essentially all of Brazil's public basic education, roughly 47 million students across more than 5,500 municipalities; FUNDEF raised per-student spending by about 40 percent between 1996 and 2000, with enrollment growth of 61 percent in the Northeast and 32 percent in the North during 1997-2002.
impactSummary: Studies credit FUNDEF with large enrollment increases in poor regions and substantial equalization of per-student spending, and quasi-experimental work finds that the exogenous teacher wage increases it generated improved student proficiency. Attribution for FUNDEB's later phases relies more on descriptive and policy analyses, and some research documents leakage and corruption in fund use in some municipalities.

name: University for All Program
summaryShort: Federal program created by Law 11.096 of January 2005 that grants full and partial scholarships to low-income students at private higher education institutions, in exchange for tax exemptions for participating institutions.
summaryLong: ProUni was created by the government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva through Law No. 11.096 of January 13, 2005. It offers full scholarships to students with per capita family income up to 1.5 minimum wages and partial (50 percent) scholarships to students with income up to 3 minimum wages, to study at private universities and colleges. Candidates must have attended public high school or held a full scholarship at a private school, and are selected based on their scores in the national secondary exam ENEM; quotas apply for Afro-Brazilian, indigenous, and disabled candidates. Participating private institutions receive exemptions from several federal taxes. Between 2005 and 2024 the program awarded more than 3.5 million scholarships, and around half of beneficiaries have been Black or mixed-race Brazilians.
objectives: Expand access to higher education for low-income graduates of public high schools
Use idle capacity in private higher education through tax-exemption incentives
Promote racial and social inclusion in higher education through reserved scholarships
Raise tertiary attainment among historically underrepresented groups
mechanisms: Private higher education institutions that join ProUni are exempted from four federal taxes in exchange for offering a set number of scholarships. Students apply through a centralized system using their ENEM scores, with eligibility based on family income and public school attendance. Full scholarships cover all tuition; partial scholarships cover half and can be combined with the FIES student loan program. Scholarships reserved for self-declared Black, mixed-race, and indigenous candidates mirror their share in each state's population.
coverage: More than 3.5 million scholarships awarded between 2005 and 2024 at over 1,000 private higher education institutions; by 2013 about 1.2 million young people had already benefited.
impactSummary: Despite its scale, ProUni has no published rigorous counterfactual impact evaluation. Available evidence is descriptive and survey-based, indicating high beneficiary satisfaction, labor market insertion of graduates, and a strong racial inclusion profile, with about half of scholarship holders identifying as Black or mixed race. Causal effects on attainment, earnings, or equity remain unquantified.

name: Basic Education Development Index
nameLocal: Indice de Desenvolvimento da Educacao Basica
summaryShort: National accountability indicator created by INEP in 2007 that combines standardized test performance (Saeb/Prova Brasil) with grade approval rates into a 0-10 score for every school, municipality, and state, with biennial targets set by the Ministry of Education.
summaryLong: The Indice de Desenvolvimento da Educacao Basica (Ideb) was created in 2007 by Brazil's national education statistics institute INEP, under the Ministry of Education's Plano de Desenvolvimento da Educacao. It synthesizes two dimensions of quality, average student performance in Portuguese and mathematics on the Saeb and Prova Brasil assessments, and school flow measured by approval rates from the School Census, into a single 0-10 indicator calculated every two years for schools, municipalities, states, and the country. The federal government set improvement targets through 2021 for every network, anchored to an aspiration of reaching the average performance of developed countries, and Ideb results are published openly and used to direct federal technical and financial support to low-performing networks. Ideb became the central accountability instrument of Brazilian basic education and a model discussed across Latin America.
objectives: Measure the quality of basic education in every school and network with a single transparent indicator
Combine learning outcomes with grade progression so schools cannot improve one at the expense of the other
Set public biennial improvement targets for schools, municipalities, and states
Guide federal support and local policy toward low-performing networks
mechanisms: Every two years INEP calculates Ideb as the product of average standardized test performance (normalized from Saeb and Prova Brasil) and the approval rate from the School Census. Results and targets for each school and network are published online. Targets set in 2007 ran through 2021, and federal programs use Ideb to prioritize technical assistance and resources. Some states have layered their own bonus and support policies on top of Ideb results.
coverage: Calculated for essentially all public and private basic education in Brazil, covering tens of thousands of schools and all 26 states, the Federal District, and more than 5,500 municipalities since 2007. In 2007-2009, over 70 percent of municipalities met or exceeded their early-primary targets.
impactSummary: Ideb is a measurement and accountability instrument rather than an intervention, and there is no consensus causal estimate of its system-wide effect. National early-primary Ideb scores rose steadily after 2007, and most municipalities met early targets, but attribution is contested. Research notes both its value as a transparent quality measure and risks of gaming through retention, exclusion, or teaching to the test.

name: Extended School Day Program
summaryShort: Policy that doubled the public school day from 4 to 8 hours with school meals included, piloted in 2011 and massively expanded after the country began allocating 4 percent of GDP to pre-university education in 2013. It now covers most public school students.
summaryLong: The Jornada Escolar Extendida began as a pilot in the 2011-2012 school year with under 9,000 students and became the flagship education policy of President Danilo Medina's government. Its rapid expansion was financed by the historic decision, won by a sustained civil society campaign (the Yellow Movement), to allocate 4 percent of GDP to pre-university education starting with the 2013 budget, as already mandated by the 1997 education law but never fulfilled; the National Pact for Education Reform signed on April 1, 2014 consolidated the commitment. Under JEE, public schools move from half-day shifts to a single 8-hour day from roughly 8am to 4pm, with breakfast, lunch, and a snack provided, additional instructional time in core subjects, and extracurricular workshops. Enrollment under the modality grew from 8,969 students in 2011-2012 to over 1.3 million students in more than 5,500 schools by 2025, about 72 percent of the public school population, supported by one of Latin America's largest school construction drives.
objectives: Extend daily instructional time in public schools from 4 to 8 hours
Improve learning outcomes in language and mathematics
Provide students with full daily nutrition through school meals
Support working families and reduce children's exposure to risks outside school
mechanisms: Schools converting to JEE abandon the traditional double-shift system and operate a single extended day of about 8 hours. The additional time is allocated to core academic subjects, tutoring, and arts, sports, and technology workshops. The school feeding institute INABIE provides breakfast, lunch, and a snack to all JEE students. Conversion required a large school construction and rehabilitation program to eliminate shared shifts, financed by the 4 percent of GDP allocation in force since 2013.
coverage: From 8,969 students in the 2011-2012 pilot to 1,346,455 students in 5,527 schools by 2025, around 72 percent of public pre-university enrollment.
impactSummary: IDB quasi-experimental studies exploiting the staggered rollout find that greater exposure to JEE reduced teenage pregnancy, while average effects on secondary test scores are small and unstable, with relevant changes in learning gender gaps. Descriptive national studies report improvements in school climate, family time organization, and nutrition. Effects on overall learning remain modest relative to the program's cost.
